newsitem.title: GERMANY: Supervisors say progress made on German bank law.
newsitem.headline: Supervisors say progress made on German bank law.

text.p: Germany's foremost bank supervisory authority said on Tuesday it had reached broad consensus with banks on the formulation of a new law governing capital adequacy requirements.

Following talks with bank associations on Monday, the BAKred supervisory body said it hoped to finalise the new legislation by mid-1997, but would give banks ample time to adapt to their changed regime.

The law -- which establishes how much capital German banks must hold to cover market risks in their trading books -- was originally due to be enforced at the start of 1996, in line with a European Union directive.
Germany is now unlikely to implement the law until 1998 at the earliest, two years behind schedule.
"What we have now is a basis for discussing a concrete proposal," said BAKred spokesman Manfred Schuboe, who noted that the outcome of the talks was "thoroughly pleasing."
The BAKred said it had managed to iron out the thorniest problems with the new law in Monday's talks.

The German Banking Association (BdB), which represents the country's leading commercial banks, had taken issue with some parts of the draft, including the need to make six-monthly reports on their market risk positions according to internationally accepted standards.

The BAKred said it had stood firm on this issue but was "fundamentally open" to the BdB's demands that small banks with minor trading activities be exempted from limits required in the law relating to interest rate and stock-market price risks.
The BdB suggested as an alternative that such banks make regular reports on their derivatives business, a suggestion which supervisors will consider in coming weeks.
The BAKred now plans to push ahead with a new proposal of the law as a whole, which will be reviewed with banks in a hearing to take place within the next few months, as is usual German practice.

Given that banks would need some time to prepare for the capital adequacy requirements even after the law is completed, it was too early to say when the law could be enforced, the BAKred's Schuboe said.
